title: A world captured by China
gist: Reviewing Tsang and Cheung's 'China's Global Strategy Under Xi Jinping', Michael Sheridan argues Xi has abandoned Deng Xiaoping's 'hide and bide' doctrine in favor of a two-pivot strategy — rallying the Global South to remake the UN order, then retaking Taiwan by force if needed — organized around the historical-mythic concept of tianxia ('all under heaven') rather than a bid to simply replace the US as global hegemon.

themes.theme: Xi's tianxia strategy and the two pivots

insights.claim: Tsang and Cheung argue that 'tianxia' (all under heaven) — a pre-modern Chinese worldview of concentric tributary circles radiating from an imperial center — is Xi Jinping's organizing principle for remaking the international order via four 'global initiatives' on governance, security, civilisation and development.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Gives investors/analysts a named ideological framework to track Chinese diplomatic and UN initiatives against, rather than treating them as ad hoc.

insights.claim: China's goal under Xi is not to replace the United States as the primary global decision-maker but to effectively remove America from that position by establishing China as a separate, parallel power centre.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: A precise framing distinct from 'China wants to be the new global hegemon' — implies China may tolerate US primacy in some domains while carving out an unchallenged parallel sphere, relevant to how investors read US-China rivalry in trade, tech and security blocs.
insights.quote: not to replace the United States as the primary decision maker on global affairs 'but to effectively remove America from that pedestal by establishing China as a separate power centre'
insights.locator: paragraph on the Chinese objective under Xi

insights.claim: The book describes a 'first pivot' to rally the Global South and reshape the United Nations to work in line with the tianxia order, followed by a 'second pivot' requiring the PLA to be ready to retake Taiwan by force once Beijing is confident of a clear UN majority supporting its claim.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Suggests a sequencing thesis for Taiwan risk: watch UN/Global South diplomatic wins as a leading indicator of timing for a Taiwan move, rather than assuming action is imminent or purely opportunistic.

insights.claim: Xi Jinping has overturned Deng Xiaoping's doctrine to 'hide our capabilities and bide our time, adroitly hide our weaknesses, do not claim leadership', replacing strategic patience with an assertive global strategy.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Marks a clear doctrinal break useful for periodizing Chinese foreign policy risk (Deng-era restraint vs. Xi-era assertiveness) in any China-exposure risk model.
insights.quote: Observe calmly, secure our position, deal with events imperturbably, hide our capabilities and bide our time, adroitly hide our weaknesses, do not claim leadership.
insights.locator: paragraph citing Deng's edict in the preface

insights.claim: A forced reunification with Taiwan (23 million people) without their consent would break the American security system in East Asia and end the decades-old concept of 'strategic ambiguity' that has preserved peace and prosperity since WWII.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Frames Taiwan not just as a regional flashpoint but as the structural anchor of the entire postwar East Asian security order — a Taiwan contingency would be a systemic, not merely regional, shock.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Obviously, the restoration of Taiwan'

insights.claim: For Xi, reunification with Taiwan would be a spectacular demonstration of power intended to project Chinese pre-eminence in both regional and global contexts, according to the authors.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Signals that a Taiwan move would be evaluated by Beijing partly as a symbolic/prestige project, not solely a strategic/territorial one — relevant to timing predictions tied to political milestones (e.g. centenary anniversaries, party congresses).
insights.quote: deliver in a spectacular way an exercise of power or authority that would project Chinese pre-eminence in both regional and global contexts
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'For Xi, the authors say'

themes.theme: Historical roots and limits of the tianxia order

insights.claim: Tianxia established a 'Pax Sinica' across East and Central Asia for more than 1,500 years, from the founding of the Han Dynasty in 202 BC to the collapse of the Qing Empire in the late 19th century under pressure from the British Empire and other powers.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete historical timeframe investors can use to understand the depth of the ideological reference Xi is drawing on, distinguishing it from a purely modern nationalist construct.

insights.claim: The authors note that Xi's peaceful framing of tianxia is contradicted by historical reality: China systematically used or threatened force to keep tributary states in line, and some of China's most creative periods of innovation occurred during eras of disunity (e.g. the Warring States period, 475-221 BC) rather than under a stable centralized order — a fact the authors say Xi's narrative suppresses.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Undercuts the CCP's own narrative that stability/unity is a precondition for prosperity and innovation, a point relevant to assessing the credibility of Beijing's stability-first governance rhetoric.
insights.quote: This peaceful image of tianxia that Xi projects was contradicted by the reality that China systematically used or threatened to use force to keep tributary states in line
insights.locator: paragraph on 'Grand Harmony' and Hu Jintao

insights.claim: Ming-dynasty Chinese fleets (1368-1644) were twice the size of the Spanish Armada and sailed as far as the Persian Gulf and East Africa, before China turned inward, destroyed its own fleets by imperial command, and stopped sending missions abroad — a historical basis for today's Chinese claim that it is not a colonialist power.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Explains the historical narrative China deploys to differentiate its expansionism from Western colonialism — relevant to understanding Beijing's messaging around Belt and Road and Global South partnerships.
insights.locator: paragraph on the Han Dynasty and Silk Road extension

themes.theme: Assessment of the book and constraints on Xi

insights.claim: The authors state plainly that 'the liberal international order is worth defending,' distinguishing themselves from peers reluctant to disturb consensus for fear of losing visas, endowments or access to China.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Signals that mainstream China-studies scholarship is often self-censoring on access/funding concerns, making this book a comparatively unfiltered data point for gauging real elite assessments of Xi's intentions.
insights.quote: The liberal international order is worth defending. It was put in place to help the world avoid the mistakes that plunged humanity into two devastating world wars in quick succession.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Unlike some of their peers'

insights.claim: As long as Xi lives and remains supreme leader, China's global strategy will remain ideologically driven by 'Xi Jinping Thought,' and the authors argue there is little the US and democratic West can do to change that trajectory.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: Implies Western China policy should plan for a multi-decade fixed strategic posture from Beijing rather than expecting near-term moderation, informing long-horizon geopolitical risk pricing.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'As long as Xi lives'

insights.claim: The authors conclude that China's radical policy ambitions can be constrained by circumstances or deterred through patient, serious diplomacy, though such deterrence may take considerable time to materialize.
insights.speaker: Michael Sheridan
insights.so_what: A cautiously optimistic policy conclusion — deterrence and patient diplomacy remain viable levers, an actionable takeaway for Western strategic planning debates on China containment.
